name: Durable Execution and Checkpointing
question: What happens when the process dies mid-task?
summary: A durable execution engine records the result of every step in an event history, so a workflow that crashes, is redeployed or waits days for a human resumes where it stopped, instead of starting over and repeating side effects. In Temporal, workflow code must be deterministic and all I/O, including model and tool calls, runs in activities with timeouts and retry policies. LangGraph offers a lighter form with checkpointers keyed by a thread id.
useCases: Long-running agents: minutes to days, with human approvals in between
Steps with side effects: payments, refunds, emails, tickets
Expensive model steps you cannot afford to repeat after a crash

items.detail: deterministic orchestration code; replayed from history after a crash
a model call, tool call or API call, with a timeout and retry policy
the recorded result of every completed step
wait for a human approval or a deadline for days, durably
LangGraph saves state after each step; resume with the same thread id
activities run at least once, so side effects still need keys (Panel 8)

steps: Put every model and tool call in an activity with a timeout and retry policy
Keep the workflow deterministic: no clocks, random numbers or I/O in it
Wait for approvals with signals or timers, not a sleeping process
Give every side-effecting activity an idempotency key
pitfalls: Assuming exactly-once: an activity can run again after a crash
Checkpointing only at the end, so a crash loses all progress
remember: Record every step. Resume, don’t restart. Keys on side effects.
caption: Illustrative: a ten-step claims job crashes at step 7; the durable version re-runs one step, a plain script all seven.

comparison.scope: Lost progress and repeated side effects

steps.title: Put every call in an activity
steps.text: Model calls, APIs and payments are activities. The workflow only orchestrates them, which keeps it deterministic and replayable.

steps.title: Timeouts and retries per activity
steps.text: The summary may take 90 seconds and is retried up to 4 times with backoff. A flaky model call no longer fails the whole claim.

steps.title: Every result goes into the history
steps.text: When an activity completes, the server appends its result to the workflow’s event history. That history, not the process memory, is the source of truth.

steps.title: Wait durably for the surveyor
steps.text: wait_condition blocks until the approve signal arrives, for minutes or days. No process has to stay alive while it waits.

steps.title: Crash, replay, continue
steps.text: If the worker dies during step 7, another worker replays the history: steps 1 to 6 return their recorded results instantly, and the workflow continues waiting for approval.

steps.title: Key the side effect
steps.text: Activities run at least once: a crash after the hospital was paid but before the result was recorded retries the payment. The key pay-CL-2291 makes the retry return the first result.

pros: Crashes and redeploys lose no progress
Waits of hours or days cost nothing
Retries and timeouts are declared, not hand-written
The event history is an audit trail of every step
cons: A new runtime to operate, or a managed service to pay for
Determinism rules constrain how workflow code is written
Still at least once: side effects need idempotency keys
avoidWhen: Short, stateless requests that finish in seconds and can simply be retried
Tasks with no side effects and cheap steps, where restarting is fine

missions.text: Crash during step 6 and run at most one step again.
missions.hint: Anything that records completed steps resumes at the step in flight.

missions.text: Crash during step 8 (the payment) without paying twice or asking the surveyor again.
missions.hint: Resume from recorded state, and give the payment an idempotency key.

missions.text: Crash at step 7 or later and resume in under a minute without repeating any model call.
missions.hint: Automatic resumption needs a durable engine, not a supervisor job.

practice.scenario: A health insurer’s cashless-claim agent runs ten steps: fetch the claim, fetch the policy, OCR the bills, summarise, screen for fraud, decide, wait for a surveyor’s approval (sometimes two days), release payment to the hospital, notify, close. It runs as a Temporal workflow, so a pod restart while waiting for approval loses nothing, and the payment activity carries an idempotency key.

industries.use: Claims that wait days for a surveyor, then release payment exactly once
Loan origination with bureau pulls, document checks and a credit-committee approval
Shipment exception handling across carriers over several days

practice.analogy: A board game saved after every move. If the power cuts out, you reload and carry on from the last move, not the first.

library.name: Temporal Python SDK
library.what: Durable workflows: every activity result is recorded in the event history; workers replay it after a crash and continue.

practice.note: Run a Worker that registers the workflow and activities on a task queue. Workflow code must stay deterministic; do all I/O in activities.

numericDrill.question: A ten-step job crashes during step 7. A plain script restarts from step 1, re-running steps 1 to 7. Steps 3, 4, 5 and 6 are model calls of 6,000 tokens each; the rest use no model. How many model tokens does the restart waste?
numericDrill.answer: The completed model steps 3 to 6 run again: 4 × 6,000 = 24,000 tokens. A durable workflow replays their recorded results from history instead, and only step 7 runs again.

interview.question: Why must Temporal workflow code be deterministic?
interview.answer: After a crash the worker replays the workflow code against the event history to rebuild its state. If the code makes different decisions on replay, for example because it reads the clock or a random number, it no longer matches the history. Put all I/O and non-determinism in activities, whose results are recorded.

interview.question: Does durable execution give exactly-once side effects?
interview.answer: No. An activity can run again if a worker crashes after the side effect but before the result is recorded. Activities are at least once, so payments, emails and tickets need idempotency keys that the receiving system honours.

mistakes.mistake: Sleeping inside a process while waiting days for approval
mistakes.fix: Wait on a durable signal or timer

mistakes.mistake: Calling APIs directly from workflow code
mistakes.fix: Do all I/O in activities with timeouts and retry policies

quiz.question: A cashless-claim job waits up to two days for a surveyor. What is the problem with a Python process that sleeps while waiting?
options: Sleeping uses too many tokens
Any restart or deploy in those two days loses the wait and the progress
Python cannot sleep for two days
The surveyor cannot see the claim
quiz.explanation: A durable signal or timer survives restarts; a sleeping process does not.

quiz.question: An 8-step loan job crashes during step 6. A plain script restarts from step 1. Steps 2, 3 and 4 are model calls of 5,000 tokens each. How many tokens of completed work are wasted?
quiz.explanation: Completed model steps 2, 3 and 4 run again: 3 × 5,000 = 15,000.

quiz.question: A Temporal activity releases a payment. The worker crashes after the bank accepted it but before the result was recorded. What happens next?
options: Nothing; Temporal guarantees exactly once
The activity may run again, so the payment needs an idempotency key
The workflow is deleted
The bank reverses the payment
quiz.explanation: Activities are at least once; the key makes the retry return the first result.

quiz.question: Which code must go in activities rather than in Temporal workflow code?
options: The order of steps
Model calls, API calls and anything else with I/O
Loops over a list already in memory
Variable assignments
quiz.explanation: Workflow code is replayed; I/O runs in activities, whose results are recorded.

quiz.question: Which of these make Temporal workflow code non-deterministic? Select all that apply.
options: Calling datetime.now()
Calling random.random()
Awaiting execute_activity for a model call
Using workflow.now()
quiz.explanation: Wall-clock time and random numbers differ on replay; activities and the workflow clock are deterministic.

quiz.question: What is Temporal’s event history?
options: The worker’s log file
A cache of model responses
The recorded sequence of a workflow’s events, including each completed activity’s result
The list of deployed versions
quiz.explanation: Replaying the history rebuilds the workflow’s state after a crash.

quiz.question: A LangGraph agent uses a Postgres checkpointer. After a pod restart, how does it continue a paused run?
options: It restarts automatically on its own
It is invoked again with the same thread id and loads the saved state
It replays the model calls
It cannot continue
quiz.explanation: Checkpointers save state per thread; something must call the graph again with that thread id.

quiz.question: A claims job crashes during the payment step. Which combination avoids both a double payment and asking the surveyor again? Select all that apply.
options: Resume from recorded state instead of restarting from step 1
Send an idempotency key with the payment
Restart the whole job from step 1
Increase the payment timeout
quiz.explanation: Recorded state keeps the approval; the key makes the repeated payment safe.

quiz.question: A returns-processing agent finishes in 3 seconds and has no side effects. Is durable execution worth it?
options: Yes, always
Probably not: a failed request can simply be retried
Yes, because it makes the model faster
No, because it cannot call models
quiz.explanation: Durable execution pays off for long, costly or side-effecting work.

quiz.question: What does a RetryPolicy with maximum_attempts=4 on a model-call activity give you?
options: Four different answers to choose from
Up to four attempts, with backoff, before the activity fails
Four parallel calls
A cap of four tokens
quiz.explanation: Transient failures are retried by the engine, not by hand-written loops.

quiz.question: A workflow waits for a customer to upload documents, with a deadline of 7 days. Which Temporal features fit?
options: A signal for the upload and a durable timer for the deadline
A while loop that polls every second
A cron job that restarts the workflow
A larger worker pool
quiz.explanation: Signals deliver events and timers enforce deadlines, both durably.

quiz.question: Which are true of activities in Temporal? Select all that apply.
options: They can be retried according to a policy
They should have timeouts
They run exactly once, guaranteed
They must avoid all I/O
quiz.explanation: Activities are where I/O belongs, with timeouts and retries; they are at least once, not exactly once.

quiz.question: A team changes the order of steps in a running workflow’s code. Why can this break in-flight workflows?
options: The server rejects all changes
Replay of existing histories no longer matches the new code
Activities stop working
Signals are lost
quiz.explanation: Workflow code changes need versioning so old executions replay with the old logic.

quiz.question: A 10-step job crashes during step 7. Under a durable workflow, how many steps run again?
quiz.explanation: Steps 1 to 6 come from history; only the step in flight, 7, runs again.

quiz.question: When is a LangGraph checkpointer usually enough, rather than a full durable engine? Select all that apply.
options: The agent pauses for a human and is resumed by the next user request
Losing a few seconds of in-flight work is acceptable
Workflows run for weeks with many timers and side effects
Resumption must happen automatically within seconds after any crash
quiz.explanation: Checkpointers suit request-driven pauses; long, timer-heavy, auto-resuming workflows suit engines like Temporal.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of the idempotency key in f"pay-{claim_id}"?
options: To speed up the payment
To make repeated payment calls for the same claim return the first result
To encrypt the claim id
To sort payments by date
quiz.explanation: The same key on a retry lets the receiving API deduplicate it.

quiz.question: Why is durable execution valuable for expensive model steps even without side effects?
options: It makes model calls cheaper per token
Completed steps are not recomputed after a crash, so their tokens are not spent twice
It removes the need for timeouts
It caches all prompts
quiz.explanation: Recorded results replace recomputation on resume.

quiz.question: A loan-origination workflow calls a credit bureau, waits for a committee, then disburses. Which design choices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Bureau call as an activity with a timeout and retries
Disbursement with an idempotency key
The committee wait as a sleeping thread
Reading the clock directly in workflow code
quiz.explanation: Activities with timeouts and keyed side effects are sound; sleeping threads and wall-clock reads in workflow code are not.

quiz.question: A rebooking workflow’s worker is redeployed mid-run. What happens under Temporal?
options: The run is lost
Another worker picks up the workflow and replays its history
The customer must start again
The server pauses until the same worker returns
quiz.explanation: Any worker on the task queue can continue the workflow from its history.

quiz.question: Which statement best contrasts durable execution with idempotency (Panel 8)?
options: They are the same thing
Durable execution resumes the workflow; idempotency makes each repeated side effect safe
Idempotency replaces durable execution
Durable execution makes idempotency keys unnecessary
quiz.explanation: You need both: resumption for progress, keys for safe repeats.
